title: Cost & Capacity Engineering
summary: The cloud bill is a system metric like latency or error rate. The best engineers reason in dollars-per-request as fluently as milliseconds-per-request.

blocks.markdown:
The cloud is a metered utility — treat the bill as a system metric you can reason about.

- You pay for **compute** (CPU/RAM time), **storage** (GB held), **network egress** (bytes leaving), and **managed services**.
- **Compute** is usually the biggest slice (~40–60%) but the easiest to cut.
- **Egress** is the line that surprises everyone — small per GB, brutal at scale.
- **Cost engineering** = do the work with the fewest, cheapest units. **Capacity engineering** = rent enough to survive peak without paying for idle metal.
- Always reason in **performance-per-dollar**, not raw speed or raw cost.

blocks.subTitle: When to reach for what
blocks.markdown:
Match the lever to the situation.

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Steady 24/7 baseline | Reserved instances |
| Spiky / unknown load | On-demand + autoscale |
| Fault-tolerant batch | Spot / preemptible |
| Hot data read by many | Caching |
| Old, rarely-read data | Tiered storage |

blocks.subTitle: The four cost buckets
blocks.markdown:
Every cloud bill decomposes into the same four buckets.

![Cloud cost broken down by resource type](assets/cost-capacity-engineering/cloud-cost-breakdown.svg)

- **Compute** — per instance-hour (or vCPU-second), scales with CPU, RAM, GPU.
- **Storage** — per GB-month for capacity held, plus a small per-operation fee.
- **Network** — nearly free inside a region; **egress** out to the internet or another region is billed per GB.
- **Managed services** — compute + storage + the provider's margin for running it.

Compute dominates; egress is the small slice that grows with traffic and careless region boundaries.

assets.alt: Cloud cost broken down by resource type

blocks.subTitle: Store cheap, move expensive
blocks.markdown:
The whole pricing model rests on one asymmetry: holding bytes is cheap, moving them is not.

- Hot object storage: **~$0.023/GB-month** — 1 TB held costs **~$23/month**.
- Cold/archive: **~$0.001–0.004/GB-month** — roughly **10x cheaper**.
- Internet egress: **~$0.05–0.09/GB** — shipping 1 TB out *once* costs **~$50–90**.
- Cross-region transfer: **~$0.02/GB** — cheaper, but easy to trigger by accident.

The provider's marginal cost lives in network links, so that's where they charge.

blocks.subTitle: Traffic cost vs data cost
blocks.markdown:
Cost grows on two different curves — track them separately.

- **Traffic-driven** (compute + egress) scales with requests/sec. It's **elastic** — rises *and* falls, so autoscaling can track it.
- **Data-driven** (storage) is a **ratchet** — it almost only goes up as you keep writing logs, uploads, and rows.
- A service can have flat traffic and a storage bill that **doubles every year**.
- That's why lifecycle/retention policies matter as much as autoscaling.

blocks.subTitle: Capacity planning
blocks.markdown:
Rent enough units to survive your busiest moment, not your average one.

![Autoscaling capacity tracking a daily demand curve](assets/cost-capacity-engineering/autoscaling-demand-curve.svg)

1. **Forecast peak**, not average — use historical peak plus growth and known events.
2. **Measure per-unit capacity** — load-test one instance for req/sec at good latency.
3. **Add headroom** — keep **20–40%** spare, plus **N+1/N+2** redundancy.
4. **Provision for peak, then autoscale down** so the floor covers baseline and the ceiling covers forecast peak.

Everything above the demand wave under a flat peak line is money paid for idle machines.

assets.alt: Autoscaling capacity tracking a daily demand curve

blocks.subTitle: Three ways to buy compute
blocks.markdown:
Three pricing models, layered together for the best deal.

- **On-demand** — full hourly rate, no commitment, off anytime. Flexible, dearest. Use for unpredictable load.
- **Reserved / committed** — commit 1–3 years for **30–70% off**. Use for the steady floor you always run.
- **Spot / preemptible** — bid on spare capacity at **60–90% off**, reclaimable with ~2 min notice. Use for fault-tolerant, stateless, interruptible work.

The winning pattern: **reserved baseline, on-demand peak, spot for burst and batch**.

blocks.subTitle: Rightsizing & tiered storage
blocks.markdown:
Two everyday levers: shrink idle compute, and demote cold data.

![Tiered storage moving data across hot, warm, and cold](assets/cost-capacity-engineering/tiered-storage.svg)

- **Rightsizing** — match instance size to real utilization. A 16-vCPU box at 8% CPU is pure waste; read weeks of metrics and shrink it.
- **Tiered storage** — recent data lives **hot** (fast SSD, high $/GB). A **lifecycle policy** ages it to **warm**, then **cold/archive** (~10x cheaper, hours to restore).

You trade access speed for storage savings on data you rarely touch.

assets.alt: Tiered storage moving data across hot, warm, and cold

blocks.subTitle: What you trade on
blocks.markdown:
Every cost lever buys savings by giving something up.

| Cheaper | Costs you |
|---|---|
| Reserved | Flexibility (locked in) |
| Spot | Reliability (can vanish) |
| Cold storage | Restore latency |
| Tight autoscaling | Scale-up lag |

Caching and CDNs spend storage/compute to slash egress. The more certain your baseline, the more you should commit.

blocks.subTitle: Decision rules
blocks.markdown:
Plain-English rules for picking a lever.

- **Steady, predictable load** → reserved. **Spiky or unknown** → on-demand + autoscale.
- **Tolerates interruption** (batch, CI, queue-backed) → spot. If a kill loses data, don't.
- **Same data read by many** → cache it before scaling the database ([caching](caching)).
- **Serving large media to users** → put a CDN in front; CDN egress is far cheaper.
- **Optimization saves less than an engineer-week** → skip it, unless it recurs forever.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
Cost-aware architecture beats penny-pinching at the largest scale.

- **Netflix Open Connect** — its own CDN with caching boxes inside ISPs, so video never pays cloud egress. Move bytes to the user to zero out the toll.
- **Dropbox Magic Pocket** — repatriated exabytes off S3 onto custom hardware, saving tens of millions. At huge steady scale, owning beats renting.
- **Amazon S3 storage classes** — Standard → IA → Glacier, with **Intelligent-Tiering** automating the lifecycle.
- **Spark on spot** — analytics clusters run on spot, checkpointing to tolerate vanishing nodes for a 60–90% discount.

blocks.subTitle: What to monitor
blocks.markdown:
Cost is invisible until it isn't. Watch the rate of change, not just totals.

- **Spend vs budget with anomaly alerts** — a >20% week-over-week jump on flat traffic is a leak.
- **Cost per unit of work** (per request, per active user) — rising unit cost means efficiency is degrading.
- **Egress by destination** — a climbing cross-region line is usually an architecture mistake.
- **Fleet utilization** — sustained <30% means rightsizing; >80% means no headroom.
- **Storage growth & tier mix** — hot growing faster than your access window means lifecycle policies aren't working.
- **Untagged spend** — where waste hides; drive it toward zero ([observability](observability)).

The cost mistakes that bite teams hardest:

- **"Optimize storage first."** Holding bytes is cheap; egress is often 3x bigger. Find the dominant bucket *first*.
- **"Autoscaling replaces capacity planning."** It tracks demand *within* the bounds you set, and scale-up isn't instant. You still size floor, ceiling, headroom.
- **"Bigger instances fix latency."** A box at 8% CPU isn't slow because it's small. Diagnose code/queries before provisioning.
- **"Reserved is always cheaper."** Only if you use it the full term. Commit to the baseline you're confident persists.
- **"Cost is finance's job."** Only engineers know which resource maps to which feature — ownership sits with them.
